sm: Destin visits WindBorne Systems in San Francisco to learn about their weather balloons. Michał and Amy explain the parts: the envelope that holds the helium, a main unit with the electronics, a sensor payload called the dangly, ballast, and a reflective pyramid shield called the Luxor that keeps the electronics warm at around minus eighty degrees. The balloons fly for weeks, going up and down to record temperature, pressure, humidity and wind in vertical profiles. A top valve vents gas to descend, and ballast is dropped to climb. Amy calls air traffic authorities before launch, and Sasha fills the balloon manually with helium and explains the red, yellow, green release sequence.

The balloon is launched, and Sasha explains it is filled only about halfway because the gas expands as pressure drops, and onboard controllers vent automatically if it climbs too high. Destin shows scuba experiments with a sealed bottle that nearly bursts at the surface and a half-filled bag that safely expands. He then builds a Cartesian diver to explain neutral buoyancy. WindBorne balloons control their buoyancy by venting gas or dropping sand, unlike ordinary weather balloons that rise until they pop. Destin shows footage from a balloon that burst and parachuted its camera back down.

Because the balloons can vent gas and drop sand, they make repeated sweeps through the atmosphere and can fly for days, weeks, or even over a year. Amy shows live data arriving by Iridium satellite roughly every seven minutes, with about 592 balloons aloft, and says each flight's ceiling depends on its envelope type. A second balloon is launched. The unit has two solar panels and a lithium battery at the center of the Luxor, which bounces the Earth's infrared radiation back to keep it warm. The record flight, called The Elder, lasted just under a year. Amy says the balloons avoid aircraft using ADS-B data and stay mostly outside normal aviation altitudes, and they launch from about sixteen sites worldwide.

Amy shows the constellation of about six hundred balloons on a map. One balloon launched from Korea had been over Greenland for twenty days, and the balloons just launched are rising over the Bay Area. She explains that a sounding is data over a column of altitude. Michał describes how the company began as a Stanford student project. The current Block 3 design uses a long string bean shaped ballast to spread out mass for aircraft safety, and Michał mentions a 737 MAX that hit space debris, which turned out to be one of their balloons.

Michał says the company learned about the strike on a Saturday evening and sent a preliminary investigation to the NTSB by Monday morning. He explains that unmanned free balloons technically have right of way, but WindBorne's balloons avoid planes by projecting uncertainty cones and taking evasive action. Chief technology officer Andrey explains that the atmosphere is like a layer cake, and vertical profiles reveal conditions such as thunderstorm potential that horizontal views miss. He shows a Thermotron temperature chamber with a vacuum chamber for calibrating sensors, down to about minus seventy degrees Celsius. The company builds about a thousand sensor boards a month, designed in house and manufactured in the United States.

Destin tours the assembly line in Redwood City, where workers build, test, seal and package the main units, add the Luxor and solar panels, and box them for launch sites. Andrey describes the balloon production line as a printing press that unrolls plastic about five times thinner than a human hair and installs the gas vent. A custom machine named Kepler uses a parabola shape to tension the plastic evenly while applying tape. The balloons are folded in a sleeve to protect them in shipping and limit flapping during launch. Dawson and others explain that the machines use three-D printed parts, were developed by trial and error, and that the workers give feedback to engineers.

Employee number one, Ken, shows how an envelope is finished, accordion folded, and tested. Co-founder Kai says about a thousand traditional weather balloons launch every day and almost none are recovered, while WindBorne's fly for months. The company funds ocean plastic removal at two kilograms for every kilogram of waste. Kai clarifies the balloons do not carry ADS-B transponders because they are power hungry and heavy, and the FAA and NORAD can see where the balloons are. Amy then demonstrates flight control. Balloons can only go up and down, so she picks winds at different altitudes, noting that winds in the central United States tend to blow west to east.

Amy picks an altitude window between about five and a half and fourteen and a half kilometers to steer a balloon toward Missouri, staying above a safe altitude to avoid cloud ice. She says she has new flight controllers crash a balloon first, because the sensors are cheap and the constellation is replaced continually. Darius explains that Tallboy balloons can be told not to vent as much to extend their lifespan. Balloons can only expend gas, and usually sand runs out first, so they fall rather than explode. Balloon 8680 reached Missouri. Anuj describes AI weather models using transformers to forecast up to fifteen days, which Destin likens to predicting the next wind vector the way language models predict the next word.

Destin compares traditional folk weather sayings to how an AI model learns which signals matter. Meteorologist Larissa explains physics-based forecasting, where the atmosphere is divided into grid cells with temperature, pressure, moisture, and wind, and equations step the state forward in small time steps. She mentions the HRRR model, a three-kilometer model over the United States. Anuj explains that AI models use the same grid as input but compress it into a coarser latent space of tensors with about a thousand dimensions, instead of solving equations. Destin says he loves how the two approaches inform each other.

Destin brings up Jevons paradox and predicts that better AI forecasting could increase demand for meteorologists, for example for wind and solar farms and agriculture. Larissa says she was once skeptical of AI forecasting, but applying physical constraints such as conservation of energy makes the models better. Anuj says AI models start from gridded states produced by physics models, and are now moving toward relying more on direct observations from satellites, balloons, ground stations and buoys. Larissa notes the company has over six hundred balloons aloft. Destin thanks Ellie for arranging the visit, mentions the hat people receive for finding a balloon, and signs off.
